objectives: Explain the social policy connections between education and politics in the United States.
Analyze historical and cultural influences and impacts on local, state, and national education, policies, and practices.
Critique the constitutional freedoms and legal protections of students and teachers.
Explain conflicts over education among local, state, and the federal government, Congress, and state legislatures.
Discuss the different and competing ideologies that inform education policy and curricular decisions.
Deconstruct historical and contemporary multicultural conflicts and public schooling.
Analyze conflicts over education and curricula initiated by external interest groups.
Critique the public-school privatization movement, its related interest groups, and the role of state legislatures and philanthropies in education reform.

objectives: Students will develop an interdisciplinary perspective - historical, philosophical, anthropological, and sociological - on race and culture in education reform and policy.
Students will develop an understanding of the policy process and efforts to create reform in education.
Students will explore the ideological basis undergirding efforts to bring about reform in education.
Students will develop critical assessments and insight regarding educational reform along with dimensions of race, culture, gender, and class.
Students will develop critical assessments of insight regarding educational reform targeted towards individuals from
various racial, cultural, ethnic, and linguistically diverse groups.

objectives: Students will interpret broad social, political, historical, economic, ecological, and land-based contexts that shape their own social classed lives and experiences.
Students will critique children’s and adult literature, media, and history through a class analysis and compare to working-class, wage-poor, and indigenous perspectives.

Students will recognize and articulate different class-based orientations in school policies and curriculum including meritocracy, neoliberalism, egalitarianism, collectivism, communalism, humanism, and posthumanism.
Students will analyze the assumptions in humanist and posthumanist theories as they are related to policies and curriculum in schools and communities.
Students will explain how ethics, ontology, and epistemology are embedded in different ways educators and youth workers approach relationships, curriculum, structures, and policies.
Students will analyze existing educational materials, environments, and curriculum from a class- and economics-focused perspective.

Students will develop and assemble educational materials that encourage expansive and critical inquiries into the way social class and economics operate in the everyday lives of youth, families, educators, and all youth…
